text:
Plant foods (Phases 2 and 5): The carnivore diet is trending, as many people (especially with leaky gut or lack of oxalate-processing bacteria) are noticing they cannot handle the fiber in plants, or the oxalates and phytates, compounds in many plants that bind minerals. It's certainly a diet worth trying, but it can lead to deficiencies over time, especially with regard to vitamins C, E, fiber, magnesium, potassium, calcium, iodine and other trace minerals, and bacteria needed to process plant foods (which already are likely missing in people who need this diet), thus making the carnivore diet sort of hard to get off.

For the most research-backed recommendations you can check this HRP deep research report. Glutamine seems worth checking into, but plant intolerance is a symptom of a variety of underlying diseases that all have different treatments.

Leaky gut (Phase 5): a widespread inflammatory condition often intersecting with other categories of illness such as Crohn's Disease or irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), plant food intolerance, and what many alternative health practitioners consider as a root cause of most diseases. It's associated with increased zonulin levels clinically. Zonulin is the molecule released to signal your intestinal tight junctions, the seals between the cells of your gut lining, to open. Too much opening time leads to allowing stuff to leak out into your blood stream which then burdens your immune system and detoxification systems. Game-changing treatments:

Liposomal first-milking colostrum (esp. fermented per Matt Nedin's protocol with bifidobacterium, a common probiotic, or SIBO yogurt bacteria). Colostrum is the first milk a cow makes after giving birth, and liposomal means it comes in tiny fat bubbles that help you absorb it. Matt from EndSickness.org finds that this helps especially to mop up mycotoxins, the toxins molds make, in the gut. Activated charcoal can also be helpful, altho don't take that with things you want to actually absorb.

Fermented veggie juices of turmeric, red cabbage, celery, beet greens (not just beet root).

Zinc carnosine, the form of zinc which sticks to your intestinal lining.

A good BPC-157 supplement, like this one from Barrier, can also help. BPC-157 is a lab-made short protein based on one in stomach juice. Note: I think Barrier's product looks smart, and their product may be really ideal, but there are some red flags in their marketing since they say it's made from plants, which is false.

Beta-glucans, a kind of fiber found in yeast extract.

Resistant starch, the starch your body can't digest, to feed the good bacteria in your gut.

Ozonated zeolite (or ZeoCharge), a volcanic mineral full of tiny pores: I find regular zeolite to be ineffective, because the pores on it are clogged up, so it can't adsorb excess zonulin, metals, and other toxins.

reader: Someone with poor gut health reading the plant-food and leaky gut causes, choosing among the leaky gut treatments the list gives.

checked.point: BPC-157 is lab-made, based on a stomach juice protein
checked.found: a synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide derived from a protein in human gastric juice (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BPC-157)
checked.still_needed: yes: it shows why the plant claim is false

checked.point: zeolite is a volcanic mineral full of pores
checked.found: porous minerals, mostly from volcanic ash (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30999685/)
checked.still_needed: yes: the pores are the point

placement: The plant-food cause and the leaky gut list, in his order; the colostrum and BPC-157 notes as sentences right after the items they explain.

questions.Q1: PASS: each term note comes right where the term first appears, or in the next sentence, and the sentence's own point still comes first; the caution's instruction now follows its warning
questions.Q2: PASS: every instruction says what it is for in the reader's terms (take it away from meals so food doesn't compete; check with your oncologist before the 5g)
questions.Q3: PASS: each term note names the exact thing (the A1 type of casein protein; the seals between the cells of your gut lining; the first milk a cow makes after giving birth)
questions.Q4: PASS: each new "it", "that" and "this" has its object in the sentence before
questions.Q5: PASS: each "so", "but" and "because" has the claim it turns on said before it
questions.Q6: PASS: the notes sit where a reader first needs them; nothing moved except the caution's instruction, up to where a reader with cancer needs it
questions.Q7: PASS: each note helps this reader act on the sentence it explains
questions.Q8: PASS: no item moved between groups
questions.Q9: PASS: the long notes are their own short sentences (stress, colostrum, BPC-157), one step each

question_text.Q1: Why am I reading this sentence, and do I know it before I have to work through it? (the point first; a study after the question it answers)
question_text.Q2: What is each instruction for, said in the reader's terms, and is it something the helper does ("have someone go with them"), not a rule stated as a fact ("someone goes with them")?
question_text.Q3: Which thing exactly? (pools of water, not water; any substance, not anything)
question_text.Q4: What does each word act on, or mean here? (adjunct remedy; known-genuine)
question_text.Q5: Why does each sentence follow from the one before? (every but, so, because and this has what it turns on)
question_text.Q6: Is this the order the reader is thinking in, and does each idea sit next to what it continues?
question_text.Q7: Does each fact help this reader now, in their case (the same kind of thing they face, not just the same topic)?
question_text.Q8: Does each item belong in the group it is put in?
question_text.Q9: Is anything compressed? (one step a sentence, the small words that carry the relation, no space before mg)
